references.text: When Israel rejected God as their king and asked Samuel for a human king, the Lord said: "It is not you they have rejected, but it is me they have rejected, so that I should not be king over them" (1 Sam 8:7). This is a direct parallel to the parable where the citizens send messengers saying, "we do not want this man to rule over us."

Israel's rebellion in the wilderness, where the people wanted to choose a new leader and return to Egypt (Num 14:4), illustrates the same motif of rejecting God's chosen leadership, just as the citizens in the parable rejected the king.
"He came to his own, and his own did not receive him" (John 1:11). The citizens in the parable who hate their master and do not want him as king reflect Israel's rejection of Jesus as the Messiah.

Jesus speaks about the world's hatred toward him and his disciples: "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you" (John 15:18-25). The word ἐμίσουν (hated) in Luke 19:14 echoes Jesus' words that the world hates him without cause.

The first Christians prayed that both Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel had gathered against God's holy servant Jesus (Acts 4:27-28). This is a historical fulfillment of the parable's image where the citizens reject the king.

In Thessalonica, the Christians were accused of acting against the emperor's decrees and saying that "there is another who is king, Jesus" (Acts 17:7). Ironically, this shows that many did not want Jesus as their king, just as the parable describes.

In Ps 2:2-3, the kings of the earth and the rulers rise up against the Lord and his anointed, saying: "Let us break their bonds apart and cast away their cords from us!" This is a prophetic description of the nations' rebellion against God's chosen king, parallel to the citizens who reject the king in the parable.

The prophecy about the Lord's suffering servant: "He was despised and rejected by men" (Isa 53:3). The hatred and rejection of the king by the citizens in the parable point toward Jesus' suffering and contempt, as Isaiah prophesied.
